cim: Angelo State University tackles the future of AI
cim_eredeti: Angelo State University tackles the future of AI
szoveg_eredeti:
Angelo State University's first faculty member dedicated specifically to artificial intelligence said AI is easily the most "disruptive innovation" of this century.

“This is one of those things that have changed the world," said Douglas G. Darby, Ph.D., of the AI Center of Excellence at ASU. "It is more powerful than anything [of similar technology] on the space shuttle.”

Darby focuses on the importance of AI knowledge, literacy, responsible application and preparedness.

"AI is something to be thoughtfully adopted, critically evaluated and responsibly guided by humans," he said.

Even considering the unknowns, “it is better to get ahead of the science,” said Darby, “than try to fix problems after they happen.”

To get ahead of the science, ASU has adopted a unique approach to AI by launching the AI COE. More than a building, the center embraces the culture of innovation and all aspects of AI technology.ed

Scarlet M. Clouse, Ed.D., dean of the College of Education and director of the Kay Bailey Hutchinson Institute, is spearheading the design and development of the center as the nucleus of knowledge and information.

On Oct. 15, a community of national and local scholars, faculty, staff and community members numbering in the hundreds convened at ASU to preview the elements of the AI COE.

“This groundbreaking initiative is transforming how we learn, teach and lead in the age of AI and is designed to make artificial intelligence accessible, ethical and impactful for all,” Clouse said.

Operating under the umbrella of the university's KBHI, “the AI COE is a bridge between theory and practice,” said Clouse.

“It empowers innovation across disciplines, industries and communities. We believe that as an AI-fluent university we should broaden that into the community and make what we do a collaboration. The success of the AI COE is built on the good relationship ASU has with the community," she said.

Clouse highlighted the AI COE Boot Camp, which pairs ASU students with local companies to solve real-world problems submitted as a Challenge. Along with learning the correct application of AI, the students and the companies collaborate to produce solutions as an offspring of the technology.

“Other Challenge opportunities will be offered to businesses in the coming months,” said Clouse.

According to the KBHI, “In less than ten years, the projected job growth for software developers will grow by nearly 18%, and more than 10% of the current workforce is already employed in AI-related roles.”

After only one year of AI undergraduate and graduate degree offerings at ASU, enrollment has increased from four students to 41, with 26 enrolled in the graduate program who have come from other bachelor’s degree fields.

As for the notion of AI taking away jobs, “every technological advance made by man suffered from the same reputation,” said Darby. “AI technology tends to create additional jobs, perhaps in a supporting role to AI or other industries.”

For those who are predisposed to a doom mentality, Darby's words “disruptive" and "powerful” might signal alarm. And there are those people who, despite empirical data, still believe the Earth is flat.

Darby encourages the community to ask questions about AI, which is already subject to unfounded claims.

“It is not conscious. It is not human. It is not evil. It may respond with human mannerisms, including peculiarities of speech such as ‘hm,’ or ‘got it,’ or sympathetic terms such as ‘sorry to hear that,'" he said.

AI is trained to include inflection and characteristics of speech to respond naturally and even informally to questions or comments. Whether or not there is danger inherent in that type of verbal exchange can be debated.

In fact, according to Darby, weaknesses in AI applications exist as human factors today and can have a negative influence on AI responses.

“Algorithms used to screen job applicants may have biases introduced by the person establishing search parameters. AI can exaggerate those biases if it detects that a certain demographic is hired in preference to another, therefore, offering only those applicants for interview that fit the bias," Darby said.

“Only by positive early human intervention in the AI development process are those problems solved from the functional to the ethical. The Angelo State University AI Center of Excellence invites everyone to participate," he said.

For more information about ASU AI curriculum offerings and the AI COE, go to angelo.edu/community/kay-bailey-hutchison-institute/innovation/ai-center-of-excellence/, or call the ASU Department of Education at 325-486-6840.
